Airway management

Patients with GCS of 8 or less may have lost pharyngeal muscle tone, cough reflex and swallow reflex (can’t protect their airway) so they need airway management

We have several different modalities of airway management

Modalities of airway management

Basic airway management:

Maneuvers: head tilt/chin lift and jaw thrust

Airway adjuncts: OPA and NPA

Advanced airway management:

EGD and ETT tube

Surgical airway: cricothyrotomy and tracheostomy

Maneuvers

Head tilt/ chin lift: it is achieved by tilting the head back while keeping the mouth closed (teeth approximated) (sniffing position)

Extension of the head lead to posterior oropharynx get further away from the base of the tongue and opens the airway; chin lift will lift the mandible which is attached to the tongue (so lifting the tongue) and opening the airway

Head tilt/chin lift is used in non trauma patients (patients with no suspected c spine injury) because this maneuver manipulate the c spine into injuring the spinal cord so jaw thrust is done instead

To perform jaw thrust in trauma patients, two emergency providers have to be involved, one to perform the jaw thrust , the other one is to stabilize the head and neck area

Jaw thrust is done by both hands on the face, palms are on the zygomatic bone and fingers lift the jaw, thumbs open the mouth

Spine motion restriction

Spine motion restriction is the maneuver done to stabilize the head and neck area in case of a suspected c spine injury

Spine motion restriction can be done by applying a rigid cervical collar (it is not enough) and furtherly stabilizing the spine using sandbags and several straps on a stretcher

Spine motion restriction can be done manually by an emergency provider by applying hands to the both sides of the head into the neck to stabilize the c spine of the patient

if the patient on cervical collar need airway management, then the collar is removed and head is stabilized manually and airway management is done and then the collar put back again

Airway adjuncts

Oropharyngeal airway (OPA)

Nasopharyngeal airway (NPA)

OPA

OPA is put to bypass the tongue (thus preventing tongue prolapse)

It will provide airway patency but not protection so it is a temporary measure

Indication of OPA is coma , when patient doesn’t have gag reflex

OPA comes in different sizes and it has to be measured from the first incisors to the angle of the jaw

if OPA size is less or more than ideal size for the patient, it might lead to airway obstruction instead of opening,

Too small might push the tongue into closing the airway

Too big might go into the esophagus and block the airway

Placement is by entering it upside down until it touch the hard palate then it is flipped and entered (to bypass the dome of the tongue)

It can also be inserted by depressing the tongue by a tongue depressor and inserting the piece

NPA

if patient does have gag reflex then OPA is contraindicated and NPA can be used instead because anything introduced nasally is less gag stimulating

NPA is longer than OPA for the same patient

Contraindications to NPA:

Basal skull fractures: patient present with symptoms such as otorrhea, raccoon eyes and battle sign. Cribriform plate could be fractured in these patients and NPA can enter the brain through the cribriform and cause brain injury

Severe midface fracture and those are commonly associated with basal skull fractures

NPA is measured from Infront of the nose and should reach the angle of the jaw or tragus of the ear

NPA is used with water soluble lubricant to prevent injury and then introduced into the nose

Device is inserted until the flared end rest against the nostril

Basic airway management

Always remember that airway maneuvers and adjuncts are just a bridge to the creation of a definitive airway

If both adjuncts are contraindicated then continue to do maneuvers until definitive airway can be done

In pediatrics maneuvers and adjuncts have to be done together to keep airway open because tongue size is big
